html:
In September 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country in the world to give all adult women the right to vote in parliamentary elections. The law was signed on 19 September, and women voted for the first time on 28 November that year.

In early colonial New Zealand, as in Europe, women had no part in politics. The campaign grew in the 1880s, led by Kate Sheppard and the New Zealand branch of the Woman's Christian Temperance Union. Many of its members wanted the vote to fight alcohol, and the liquor trade fought back hard.

How it was won:

  • Huge petitions to Parliament, the last in 1893 with nearly 32,000 signatures, almost a quarter of the colony's adult European women.
  • Allies among male politicians, some of whom thought women would vote liberal, others conservative.
  • A narrow vote in the upper house, where two opponents of the bill changed sides, partly in anger at the tactics of premier Richard Seddon, who had tried to kill it.

Māori women voted too, in the separate Māori seats. Women could not yet stand for Parliament; that came only in 1919. In 1893 Elizabeth Yates also became mayor of Onehunga, the first woman mayor in the British Empire.

New Zealand's example, part of the democratic experiments of the Australasian colonies that also gave the world the secret ballot, encouraged suffrage campaigners elsewhere. South Australia followed in 1894 and gave women the right to stand for parliament as well. Kate Sheppard's face is on the New Zealand ten-dollar note.
